chapter_title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 18 periods = 720 minutes
Total: 18 periods · 12h 0min

periods.activity_description: Students examine three everyday mixtures — grains with small stones, salt dissolved in water, and iron nails mixed with sawdust — and describe what they observe about each component: its size, appearance, whether it dissolves, and whether a magnet attracts it.

roles.role_description: Provides the three sample mixtures and guides students to make structured observations using a prompt card.
Examine each mixture and record observable properties of each component on a shared observation sheet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the chapter's framing question — why do we need to separate mixtures — and distributes the three sample mixtures to groups.
Groups examine each mixture and record observable properties: size difference, solubility in water, response to a magnet, and density clue (does one component float?).
Groups share one striking observation per mixture in a brief whole-class round; teacher notes recurring property words on the board without yet naming methods.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's opening unit, so orient students to the central question: when substances are mixed, their physical differences are the key to pulling them apart. Watch for students who conflate 'dissolves' with 'disappears permanently' — the salt-in-water mixture is the first place to gently probe that idea without resolving it yet. A useful checkpoint before closing is whether every group can name at least two observable properties that differ between the components of one mixture.
materials: Small tray of rice mixed with pebbles
Jar of iron nails mixed with sawdust

periods.activity_title: Handpicking and the Peanut Skin Blow
periods.activity_description: Students rub peanuts between their palms to loosen the skins (replicating Activity 9.1) and then blow air to separate the lighter skins from the heavier kernels, before manually picking out a few black pepper corns from a small rice sample — directly experiencing the role of size, colour, and weight differences in separation.

roles.role_description: Performs the peanut-rubbing and blowing action, then handpicks pepper from rice, recording what property made each task possible.
Circulates to prompt students to articulate which observable property of each component enabled the separation.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's property list from the board and poses the question: what happens when the unwanted component is very small in quantity?
Each student rubs a small handful of peanuts, blows the skins away, and records which property made blowing work; then handpicks pepper from a rice sample and names the property used.
Students pair up and compare their property explanations, then agree on a single sentence explaining why handpicking is useful only when the quantity is small and components differ visibly.
Pairs share their sentences; teacher draws out the idea that every method exploits a specific property difference, setting up the classification work ahead.

periods.teacher_notes: Building directly on the observation list from the previous unit, this unit asks students to feel the property difference rather than only see it. A common error here is for students to say they separated 'because the pepper is black' without articulating that the relevant property is colour difference combined with size — press them to be specific. Groups that finish the peanut task quickly can be asked whether the method would still work if the quantity of skins were very large.
materials: Small plate of rice with a few black peppercorns

periods.activity_description: Teacher demonstrates threshing by beating a small bundle of dried grass stalks against a wooden block so seeds detach, then demonstrates winnowing by blowing husk from grain on a tray, and finally demonstrates sieving by passing whole wheat flour through two sieves of different mesh size, so students observe how particle size and air flow drive these separations.

roles.role_description: Performs all three demonstrations sequentially, pausing after each for students to sketch and label what they observe.
Sketches each demonstration setup and writes one property (size, weight, air-flow response) that makes each separation possible.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects this unit to the previous two: those units used hands and breath; today's demonstrations show how the same property principles scale up to farm-level methods.
Threshing demonstration: teacher beats the grass bundle, students sketch the before-and-after and note that grains detach because the stalk connection is weak.
Winnowing demonstration: teacher pours grain-and-husk mix from a height over the tray while blowing; students note that the lighter husk is carried away while the heavier grain falls straight.
Sieving demonstration: teacher passes flour through two sieves; students observe which particles pass and which are retained, then write one sentence linking mesh-hole size to particle size.

periods.teacher_notes: Students have now met handpicking and blowing-by-hand in the previous two units; this unit shows the same property logic operating at a larger scale. A misconception to watch for during winnowing is that students may think the grain sinks because it is 'sticky' rather than because it is heavier — redirect by asking which component they think would move more if you fanned both equally hard. The sketch-and-label pause after each demonstration is the checkpoint: every student should be able to label the component that moves and name the property driving it.
materials: Small bundle of dried grass or millet stalks with seeds
Two sieves of different mesh sizes

periods.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
periods.activity_description: Students receive cards describing six mixture scenarios and must classify each scenario under the property that makes a separation possible — size difference, weight or density difference, solubility difference, or magnetic character — before they name any method, practising property-first reasoning.

roles.role_description: Sort the six scenario cards into property categories and write a justification sentence for each placement.
Circulates, asking probing questions when a group's justification relies on method name rather than property.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the shift from the first stage: 'We have seen several separations — now the question is what property is doing the work.' Distributes scenario cards and four labelled property envelopes.
Groups sort all six cards, write a justification sentence on the back of each card, and flag any card where they are uncertain which property applies.
Each group presents one card they found easy and one they found difficult; class negotiates the correct category for disputed cards with teacher facilitation.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 2 by asking students to reason about properties before reaching for method names — that sequence is the conceptual heart of the chapter. A common error is placing the salt-water scenario under 'size difference' because solid and liquid are different; redirect by asking whether the salt particles are actually visible and larger than the water. Groups ready to move on can be asked to add a fifth property envelope of their own devising if they think any scenario doesn't fit the four provided.
materials: Six scenario cards (rice and pebbles; grain and husk; iron nails and sawdust; salt in water; mud in water; butter in curd)

periods.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
periods.activity_description: Students add a spoonful of soil to a jar of water, stir, allow the mixture to stand, observe the sediment form at the bottom, and then carefully pour the clearer upper liquid into a second container — directly experiencing sedimentation and decantation and recording which property (insolubility and density greater than water) determines whether a component settles.

roles.role_description: Carry out the stirring, waiting, and pouring steps, recording observations at each stage on a structured observation sheet.
Guides the class through a timed observation at each stage and asks groups to articulate why the soil sinks rather than stays dispersed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit's property-card work: 'Mud-in-water was in your density/weight envelope — today we watch that property doing the work.' Groups prepare jars.
Students add soil to water, stir vigorously, and record an immediate observation; they then allow the mixture to stand and record a second observation when sediment is visible.
Groups carefully pour the upper liquid into a second clean container, record how much sediment remained, and note that some very fine particles may still be suspended.
Brief discussion: why does decantation not separate all particles? Students predict what extra step might separate the remaining fine particles — priming the next unit on filtration.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently assume that decantation gives completely clean water; the visible cloudiness of the decanted liquid is important evidence to dwell on — it sets up the need for filtration in the next unit. Watch for the misconception that only very large particles can sediment; even moderately fine sand will settle given enough time, and the chapter is explicit that decantation is not complete. The predictive question at the close ('what extra step would work?') is a useful readiness probe for the filtration unit ahead.

periods.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
periods.activity_description: Students fold a filter paper into a cone, seat it in a glass funnel over a conical flask, and pour the muddy water from the previous unit through it — collecting mud as the residue on the filter paper and clear water as the filtrate in the flask, observing how pore size governs what passes through.

roles.role_description: Assemble the filtration setup, pour the muddy water through, observe the residue and filtrate, and compare the clarity of the filtrate to the decanted liquid from the previous unit.
Demonstrates correct filter-paper folding technique before groups begin and circulates to ensure funnels are properly seated.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates filter-paper folding (fold in half twice, open one layer to form a cone) while linking to students' prediction from the previous unit that a finer barrier would separate remaining particles.
Groups assemble the filtration apparatus, pour the muddy water through, and observe both the residue collecting on the paper and the filtrate dripping into the flask.
Groups compare the clarity of the filtrate against the decanted sample from the previous unit and write one sentence explaining why filtration removes particles that decantation cannot.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the sedimentation–decantation–filtration sequence; the comparison of filtrate clarity to decanted clarity is the pivotal observation, so encourage groups to hold both containers against the light together. A frequent error is tearing the filter paper by pouring liquid directly onto it rather than against the funnel wall — remind students to pour gently along the side. Students who see that the pore size of the filter paper is doing the separating are ready to move into Stage 3's method-selection reasoning.
materials: Clear comparison beaker of decanted water

periods.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
periods.activity_description: Groups plan and construct a working multi-layer water filter from low-cost materials (gravel, sand, cotton, charcoal in a cut plastic bottle), predict which layer will remove which size of particle based on the pore-size principle from the previous unit, and test it with muddy water.

roles.role_description: Design the layer order, justify each layer's placement based on particle-size reasoning, assemble the filter, test it, and evaluate whether the output matches their prediction.
Provides materials and prompts groups to justify layer order before building, ensuring reasoning is explicit rather than trial-and-error.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit: 'Filter paper separates by pore size — now you will design a system using everyday materials and the same principle.' Groups list the available materials and their estimated pore sizes.
Groups decide on layer order with written justification, assemble the filter in a cut bottle, and test it by pouring muddy water through.
Groups compare predicted and actual output clarity, note which layer they think did the most work, and share one design revision they would make if they repeated the task.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established pore-size as the operative principle; this unit asks students to extend that reasoning to a multi-layer system where each layer targets a different particle size. Watch for groups that place the finest layer (cotton or filter paper) at the top — they will quickly observe that coarse particles clog it; this is a productive error worth discussing rather than pre-empting. A group that can articulate why the coarse layer should go first has genuinely internalised the pore-size classification from Stage 2.

periods.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
periods.activity_description: Students use a simple churner (or two sticks twisted together) to churn a small quantity of full-fat curd, observing that butter — lighter and less dense — gradually collects at the surface and can be skimmed off, while buttermilk remains, linking the separation to density difference.

roles.role_description: Take turns churning the curd, observe the gradual appearance of butter at the surface, skim it off, and record which property of butter (lower density) allowed it to separate.
Introduces the term 'churning' and asks students to connect the property responsible to the property-card categories from the earlier unit in this stage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the property-card unit: butter-in-curd was in the density/weight envelope — today groups will see why by actually churning.
Groups churn curd using the mathni or twisted-stick method, observing in real time where the butter accumulates and recording observations at intervals.
Students skim off the butter, compare the remaining buttermilk to the original curd in texture and appearance, and write one sentence connecting the separation mechanism to density difference.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often expect churning to work quickly; in practice the butter appears gradually, which itself reinforces that the property difference (density) is small and requires mechanical action to exploit. A misconception to anticipate is that churning 'makes' the butter rather than separating something already present in the curd — ask students whether butter existed in the curd before churning to probe this. This is the final activity that populates the density-difference branch of the classification arc before the class moves to evaporation and magnetic separation.

periods.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
periods.activity_description: Students spread a few drops of salt solution on dark paper and allow the water to evaporate at room temperature, observing the white salt residue that forms as the water vapour escapes — directly experiencing that evaporation converts liquid water to vapour and leaves the dissolved solid behind.

roles.role_description: Spreads the salt solution on dark paper, monitors the drying process, and records the observation that white residue appears as the water disappears.
Frames the unit by asking why neither handpicking, sieving, nor filtration would work for the salt-water mixture, creating a conceptual need for a new mechanism.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the property-card unit and asks why none of Stage 2's methods work for dissolved salt — drawing out that filtration only catches visible particles and salt particles are too small.
Each student spreads a few drops of salt solution on dark paper and sets it aside to dry; while waiting, they write a prediction of what will remain and what will leave.

Students examine their dried papers, sketch and describe the white residue, and write a sentence distinguishing what happened to the water (it became vapour) from what happened to the salt (it stayed as solid).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 3 and introduces a conceptually distinct mechanism — a physical change in the state of the liquid — rather than a physical barrier. Students commonly predict that the salt also disappears with the water; the white residue on dark paper is the key contradicting observation to linger on. Connecting explicitly to the salt-in-water card from the property-card unit helps students see that the dissolved-solid property is what makes evaporation the appropriate method.
materials: Dark construction paper or black card

periods.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
periods.activity_description: Students heat a small amount of salt solution in a china dish over a spirit lamp, observing the water boiling away and the dry salt residue forming in the dish — comparing the speed and completeness of evaporation by heating to the slow room-temperature evaporation from the previous unit.

roles.role_description: Heat the salt solution under supervision, record observations as the liquid level drops and bubbles appear, and sketch the residue left when all liquid has boiled away.
Supervises spirit lamp use, directs attention to the steam rising from the dish, and asks students to connect the steam to the concept of water converting to vapour.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit: 'Room-temperature evaporation was slow — today we speed it up with heat and watch the same process more clearly.' Groups set up china dishes and spirit lamps.
Groups heat the salt solution, recording observations at intervals: steam rising, liquid level dropping, crystals appearing, and finally a dry salt residue remaining in the dish.

Groups compare their heated-evaporation residue to their room-temperature paper residue from the previous unit and write one sentence explaining what the liquid water became — formally defining evaporation as conversion of liquid to vapour.

periods.teacher_notes: The parallel between slow (room temperature) and fast (heated) evaporation is pedagogically important: students should see these as the same physical change at different rates, not two different processes. A misconception to watch for is that the salt 'burns away' when heated — the absence of any charring and the clean white residue are evidence against this. Students who can articulate that the water underwent a change of state while the salt did not have grasped the core of this stage's LO.

periods.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
periods.activity_title: Seawater to Salt — The Industrial Scale
periods.activity_description: Teacher explains how shallow coastal salt pans exploit solar evaporation at scale — seawater flows into shallow pits, sunlight and wind drive off the water as vapour over days, leaving a solid mixture from which salt is then purified — connecting the bench-top observations from the previous two units to a real industrial process.

roles.role_description: Presents a diagram of salt pans, explains the role of sunlight and wind in accelerating evaporation, and connects each element to what students observed with the spirit lamp and dark paper.

Annotates a simplified salt-pan diagram, labelling what enters (seawater), what leaves as vapour (water), and what remains (solid salt mixture), and writes one sentence explaining why this counts as a physical — not chemical — change.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the salt-pan context and diagram, linking sunlight-as-heat and wind-as-carrier to the spirit lamp and open air the students have already used.
Students annotate their diagram individually, labelling inputs, outputs, and the change of state that drives the process.
Students share their annotations in pairs, resolve any differences, and identify one similarity and one difference between the lab activity and the industrial salt-pan process.

periods.teacher_notes: After two hands-on units, this didactic unit consolidates the evaporation concept at real-world scale; the diagram annotation is the active task that prevents it from becoming purely passive. Students sometimes wonder why the salt is described as a 'solid mixture' that still needs purification — note that seawater contains other dissolved substances besides salt, so the first evaporation step separates liquid from solids but not one solid from another. This is a useful conceptual boundary to mark before the class moves into Stage 4.
materials: Printed or drawn diagram of coastal salt pans

periods.stage_label: Investigate magnetic separation and extend the property-to-method classification
periods.activity_description: Students pass a bar magnet slowly through a tray of iron nails mixed with sawdust, observing which component is attracted to the magnet and which is not — then vary the experiment by testing three other small objects (aluminium foil, a copper coin, a steel pin) to establish which substances are magnetic.

roles.role_description: Perform the magnet-pass, record which objects are attracted, and classify each tested substance as magnetic or non-magnetic.
Introduces the term 'magnetic substance' after groups have completed their classification, connecting it to iron as the primary example in the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to Stage 2's property-card work: the iron-nails-in-sawdust card was in the 'magnetic character' envelope — today groups investigate what that means in practice.
Groups pass the magnet through the iron-nails-and-sawdust mixture, then test aluminium foil, a copper coin, and a steel pin, recording attracted or not-attracted for each.
Groups write a classification: 'magnetic substances' versus 'non-magnetic substances', and then write one sentence explaining the key property that makes magnetic separation possible.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens Stage 4, which extends the property-to-method map to magnetic character and then moves toward integrated selection reasoning. Students often assume all metals are magnetic — aluminium and copper will likely surprise groups who hold this idea, making those test objects especially important. The sentence-writing step is the conceptual payoff: students should be able to say that magnetic separation works because the two components differ in their response to a magnetic field, not simply that 'iron sticks to magnets'.

periods.stage_label: Investigate magnetic separation and extend the property-to-method classification
periods.activity_title: Industrial Magnets and the Complete Property Map
periods.activity_description: Teacher explains how cranes fitted with large electromagnets separate scrap iron from heaps of industrial waste for recycling, then guides students to complete a full property-to-method reference map that captures all nine separation methods covered so far alongside the property that makes each one possible.

roles.role_description: Presents the industrial magnetic crane context and then leads a structured whole-class mapping exercise, calling on students to supply each entry.
Fills in a pre-printed property-to-method table as entries are confirmed by the class, producing a personal reference map for the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the industrial magnetic crane example, asking students to identify what property of scrap iron makes this effective — bridging from the small-scale inquiry in the previous unit.

Teacher and class co-construct the full property-to-method map on the board; students fill in their individual pre-printed tables, adding the property, the method, and a one-word example for each row.
Students scan their completed tables and identify which property column has the most methods assigned to it, writing a sentence explaining why density and weight differences support so many methods.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates Stage 4 by making the property-to-method map explicit as a single reference, drawing together everything from handpicking to magnetic separation. Students often place threshing and winnowing in the same cell as handpicking under 'size'; challenge them to distinguish — threshing exploits mechanical detachment rather than a property difference between already-separate components. The observation that density supports multiple methods is a genuine and useful generalisation, not just a counting exercise.

periods.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
periods.activity_title: Method-Selection Reasoning — Why This, Not That?
periods.activity_description: Students receive eight mixture scenario cards and must select the correct separation method for each, then write a two-part justification: which property of the components makes this method possible, and why at least one other method would fail for this mixture.

roles.role_description: Select the method for each scenario, write the two-part justification, and flag any scenario where they debated between two methods.
Circulates and probes groups on their 'why this method fails' reasoning, ensuring students are not just retrieving correct answers but constructing causal explanations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames Stage 5: 'Knowing all the methods and knowing which property each exploits is preparation — now we use that to reason about unfamiliar mixtures.' Distributes the eight scenario cards.
Groups work through all eight scenarios, selecting the method and writing the two-part justification for each; they mark any scenario they found genuinely ambiguous.
Groups share their ambiguous scenarios with the class; teacher facilitates discussion of cases where more than one method might apply and what factors would decide between them.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the first unit of Stage 5, and the two-part justification structure is the key move: selecting the right method is the easy half; explaining why an alternative fails is the reasoning demand. Watch for groups that explain failure purely in terms of practicality ('filtration would be too slow') rather than property mismatch ('filtration would not work because salt particles are too small to be caught by the pore'). The ambiguous scenarios — particularly any involving decantation versus filtration — are worth class time because they reveal how multiple properties can be simultaneously relevant.
materials: Property-to-method reference maps from the previous unit

periods.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
periods.activity_description: Students play the chapter's consolidation matching game (Activity 9.6) pairing separation scenarios to methods, then extend it by generating two novel scenarios of their own — one for which a method they choose is clearly correct and one for which no single method from the chapter is sufficient — defending both choices in writing.

roles.role_description: Complete the matching game, then author two novel scenarios with written defence of method choice or explanation of why no single method suffices.
Monitors the extension task to ensure student-authored scenarios are grounded in real mixtures and the property logic of the chapter, not arbitrary combinations.

time_bands.activity: Groups complete the Activity 9.6 matching game, cross-checking answers against their property-to-method reference maps.
Each group authors two novel scenarios and writes their written defence for each.
Groups swap their novel scenarios with an adjacent group and attempt to match methods; the authoring group then reveals and explains their intended answers.

periods.teacher_notes: The matching game serves as a quick retrieval check; the extension is where the genuine reasoning demand of Stage 5 lives. Students sometimes struggle to construct a scenario where no single method suffices — guide them to think about multi-component mixtures, such as a mixture of sand, salt, and iron filings, where separation requires sequencing methods. The scenario-swap closure is both a peer-assessment move and a check that the authored scenarios are unambiguous enough for others to reason about.

periods.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
periods.activity_description: Students receive three complex mixture problems — each containing three or more components requiring more than one separation method applied in sequence — and must plan the sequence, justify each step by naming the property exploited, and identify what would go wrong if the steps were reordered.

roles.role_description: Independently plans the separation sequence for each problem and writes a step-by-step justification before sharing with a partner.
Compares plans in pairs, resolves differences, and prepares a shared sequence to present to the class.
Selects two contrasting pair-plans for the same problem and facilitates a class discussion about which sequence is better and why.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the sequencing challenge: 'When a mixture has three components, the property-to-method map must be applied in the right order.' Distributes the three problems.
Students work individually on all three problems, writing a step-by-step sequence with property justification for each step.
Students pair up, compare sequences, resolve differences by arguing from the property map, and produce a shared final sequence.
Teacher presents two contrasting solutions for one problem on the board and class discusses which order is correct and what goes wrong if steps are swapped.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units exercised single-method selection; this unit pushes students to reason about ordering, which requires holding multiple property differences in mind simultaneously. A rich problem to select for the class discussion is one where magnetic separation must come before evaporation — if salt is evaporated first, the iron filings would be embedded in the salt residue and harder to magnetically extract. Watch for students who sequence steps correctly but cannot articulate why the order matters; that articulation is the hallmark of Stage 5 reasoning.
materials: Three complex mixture problem cards (each with 3+ components)

periods.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
periods.activity_description: Groups receive a mixture of iron filings, sand, and salt and must apply a self-chosen sequence of magnetic separation, filtration, and evaporation to recover all three components separately — executing the reasoning from the previous unit as a practical investigation.

roles.role_description: Execute the planned separation sequence, recording each step's yield, and evaluate at the end whether their chosen order was optimal.
Provides materials and challenges groups to defend their chosen sequence before they begin, then circulates to observe where the sequence breaks down if misordered.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks each group to state their intended sequence and the property justification for the first step before any materials are touched — a brief verbal check before execution begins.
Groups carry out the separation in their chosen sequence: passing a magnet to remove iron filings, filtering the remaining sand-salt water mixture, then evaporating to recover the salt.
Groups assess their recovered components, note any losses or contamination, and write one sentence on whether their sequence was optimal or whether a different order would have worked better.

periods.teacher_notes: This practical unit is the pay-off for the planning unit that preceded it; if the verbal check at the start reveals a group with a confused sequence, this is the moment to redirect before they waste materials. A common practical error is filtering before removing iron filings — the filings can clog the filter paper, making this a productive failure to discuss if it occurs. The self-evaluation sentence at the close is important: students who can identify what went wrong and why are demonstrating exactly the integrated reasoning the dissolution test targets.
materials: Mixture of iron filings, sand, and salt (per group)

periods.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
periods.activity_description: Groups examine four real-world separation scenarios drawn from the chapter — salt from seawater, butter from curd, iron from industrial waste, husk from grain — and for each, identify every observable property difference present in the mixture, select the method that exploits the most decisive property, and propose an alternative method and explain why it would be less effective.

roles.role_description: Analyse each scenario, produce a written property-method-alternative response for each, and present one scenario to the class with full justification.
Facilitates presentations, probing the alternative-method reasoning to surface any remaining gaps in property-to-method logic.

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames the closing unit: groups will apply everything built across the chapter to real scenarios from the chapter's own narrative, reasoning from properties to methods to alternatives.
Groups produce written property-method-alternative responses for all four scenarios, drawing on their property-to-method reference maps.
Each group presents one assigned scenario; class evaluates whether the alternative-method reasoning correctly identifies a property mismatch, with teacher facilitating brief corrections where needed.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit draws together the full arc from Stage 1's raw observations to Stage 5's property-grounded method selection and comparative evaluation. The alternative-method reasoning is the highest-demand move in the chapter, so probe it actively during presentations — students should be explaining a property mismatch, not just saying the alternative 'would not work'. If a group's alternative-method explanation is merely practical ('too slow') rather than principled ('wrong property'), that is the final misconception to correct before the chapter closes.
materials: Four real-world scenario cards (salt from seawater, butter from curd, iron from industrial waste, husk from grain)

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine, handle, and observe three types of everyday mixtures and experience handpicking, blowing, threshing, winnowing, and sieving directly, recording what they can see, feel, and notice about each component.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the observable characteristics — size, colour, weight response to air, and ability to be manually distinguished — of components in at least three everyday mixtures encountered in the chapter.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify mixtures by the physical property that enables separation
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify mixture scenarios by the physical property that makes separation possible — size, density, pore-size filtration, or magnetic character — through property-card sorting, sedimentation and decantation observation, laboratory filtration, water-filter design, and churning.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given mixture into a property category (size difference, density difference, solubility, or magnetic character) and explain which observable physical property of the components makes a stated separation method applicable.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe salt residue forming as water evaporates at room temperature and by heating, annotate a salt-pan diagram, and explain that evaporation converts liquid water to vapour — a physical change of state — leaving the dissolved solid behind.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe evaporation as the conversion of liquid water to water vapour and explain how this physical change of state separates a dissolved solid from a liquid, citing evidence from at least one observation.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Investigate magnetic separation and extend the property-to-method classification
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students investigate which substances are attracted to a magnet, classify them as magnetic or non-magnetic, and complete a full property-to-method reference map covering all nine separation methods from the chapter.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify substances as magnetic or non-magnetic based on observed response to a magnet and can populate a complete property-to-method map that correctly assigns all nine chapter separation methods to the physical property each exploits.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students select and justify separation methods for single and multi-component mixtures by reasoning from observable physical properties — including differences in size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — execute a three-component practical separation, and evaluate alternative methods by identifying which property difference each would fail to exploit.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can select and apply the appropriate separation method for a given mixture by identifying the decisive observable physical property difference between its components — including size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — and can justify why an alternative method would be less effective for that mixture.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the observable characteristics — size, colour, weight response to air, and ability to be manually distinguished — of components in at least three everyday mixtures encountered in the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: When a student blows on a mixture of peanut kernels and their lighter skins, the skins fly away while the kernels stay on the tray. Which observable characteristic of the components is being exploited in this separation?

options.label: A
options.text: Difference in colour between the skin and the kernel

options.label: B
options.text: Difference in response to moving air due to unequal weight

options.label: C
options.text: Difference in solubility when the skins are wet

options.label: D
options.text: Difference in the size of pores through which the skins can pass

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing colour indicates the student noticed the visual difference but conflated an incidental observable property with the operative mechanism; colour is not what air-flow acts upon.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing solubility shows the student is confusing the peanut-blowing observation with the dissolved-salt scenario, misapplying a property from a different mixture context in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing pore size shows the student is mapping the sieving/filtration concept onto this scenario, confusing a physical barrier mechanism with an air-flow mechanism.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who initially chose colour can be redirected by asking what would happen if both components were the same colour — would blowing still work? Students who prefer kinaesthetic reasoning can replay the peanut-blowing activity and focus on which component their breath moves more.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the observable characteristics — size, colour, weight response to air, and ability to be manually distinguished — of components in at least three everyday mixtures encountered in the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: A farmer uses a soop (bamboo tray) to toss a mixture of grain and husk into the breeze. The husk blows away while the grain falls back into the tray. What observable characteristic of the grain allows it to fall back down?

options.label: A
options.text: The grain dissolves in the moisture in the air and falls back as drops

options.label: B
options.text: The grain is heavier than the husk and is not carried by the breeze

options.label: C
options.text: The grain is larger in size than the husk

options.label: D
options.text: The grain is magnetic and is attracted back to the tray

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing size shows the student is conflating the sieving principle (size difference as a physical barrier) with the winnowing principle (weight difference in air), a common confusion between two chapter methods.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing magnetic attraction is an implausible cross-method confusion — the student is retrieving 'something pulls the grain back' from the magnetic separation section without evaluating plausibility.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing dissolution reflects a fundamental misunderstanding that grains can dissolve, possibly from the evaporation section's emphasis on salt dissolving in water.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose size can be asked to consider what would happen if grain and husk were the same size but different weights — would the farmer's tossing still work? Students with stronger kinaesthetic reasoning can mime the tossing action and identify which component they feel is harder to lift.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Mixture | Method tried | Result
Sand in water | Decantation | Sand settled; upper water poured off — some fine particles remained
Sand in water | Filtration | Clear water collected in flask; all sand retained on filter paper

assessment_items.question_text: A student tested two mixtures with two separation methods each. Refer to the table provided. Which statement best explains why filtration removed sand from water but did not remove salt from water?

options.label: A
options.text: Salt dissolves in the water that passes through the filter, carrying it along

options.label: B
options.text: Sand is heavier than salt, so it gets caught on the filter paper more easily

options.label: C
options.text: Sand particles are large enough to be retained by the pores of the filter paper, whereas dissolved salt particles are too small to be caught

options.label: D
options.text: The filter paper absorbs salt and lets sand through because sand is a solid

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing weight shows the student is confusing the operative property (particle size relative to pore size) with density/weight, carrying over the density reasoning from the winnowing and decantation context.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'salt dissolves and is carried through' shows the student has a partially correct understanding — salt does pass through — but misattributes the reason to an active dissolving event during filtration rather than to particle size being smaller than pores.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'filter paper absorbs salt' reflects an invented mechanism not grounded in the chapter and shows the student does not yet have a pore-size model of filtration.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose option C are close to the correct idea; ask them whether salt would pass through the filter even if it had not been dissolved — this redirects them to particle size as the governing property. Students who benefit from visual reasoning can examine the filter paper and funnel assembly from the hands-on unit and count (conceptually) what size of particle could pass through the pores.

assessment_items.question_text: Butter rises to the top and can be skimmed off after curd is churned. Which physical property of butter is directly responsible for this separation?

options.label: A
options.text: Butter has a larger particle size than buttermilk and cannot pass through the churner's gaps

options.label: B
options.text: Butter is lighter (less dense) than buttermilk and therefore floats to the surface

options.label: C
options.text: Butter is magnetic and is drawn upward when the churner rotates

options.label: D
options.text: Butter is white in colour, making it visually distinct from the buttermilk

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing colour shows the student is applying an irrelevant observable property — colour helps identification but is not the mechanism of separation in churning.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing magnetic shows a cross-method confusion, possibly because the student recalled that churning involves mechanical rotation and associated rotation with magnets from the magnetic separation section.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing particle size shows the student is applying the sieving/filtration principle to churning, confusing a density-driven separation with a size-exclusion separation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose particle size can be asked whether a sieve would separate butter from buttermilk — if not, why not? This redirects attention to density as the operative property. Students who prefer concrete examples can be asked to recall any time they saw oil floating on water and identify which property causes that, then apply the same reasoning to butter and buttermilk.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: A student pours muddy water into a jar and lets it stand. After some time, she pours the clearer upper water into a second jar. She notices the second jar still looks slightly cloudy. She then pours this slightly cloudy water through a filter paper in a funnel. The water collected in the flask below is now clear. Explain, using the concept of particle size, why decantation alone did not make the water completely clear but filtration did.
expected_elements: Decantation separates particles that are heavy enough to settle (sediment) to the bottom of the liquid, but very fine particles remain suspended and do not settle, leaving the water cloudy.

Filtration works by passing the liquid through the small pores of the filter paper; particles that are larger than the pores are retained on the paper even if they were too light to settle by decantation.
The filter paper therefore removes the remaining fine particles that decantation could not, resulting in clear water in the flask.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write a connected explanation can be asked to answer in two separate sentences: 'What does decantation leave behind?' and 'What does the filter paper catch?' This scaffolds the same reasoning in shorter steps. Students with stronger verbal reasoning can be encouraged to use an analogy comparing the filter paper's pores to a very fine net.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evaporation as the conversion of liquid water to water vapour and explain how this physical change of state separates a dissolved solid from a liquid, citing evidence from at least one observation.

competency.competency_text: Description of physical changes in matter

assessment_items.question_text: A student spreads a few drops of salt solution on dark paper and leaves it in sunlight. After some time, white patches appear on the paper where the drops were. What does the appearance of white patches tell us about what happened to the water and the salt?

options.label: A
options.text: The salt evaporated along with the water and then fell back as white patches when the vapour cooled

options.label: B
options.text: The sunlight chemically changed the salt solution into a new white substance on the paper

options.label: C
options.text: The water evaporated — it converted to water vapour and left the paper — while the salt remained as a solid residue

options.label: D
options.text: The water was absorbed into the dark paper, pulling the salt with it and then releasing it on the surface

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing absorption shows the student does not have a model of evaporation as a change of state; they are explaining the disappearance of liquid through absorption rather than conversion to vapour.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'salt evaporated and fell back' reveals the misconception that salt also undergoes evaporation — this is addressed directly in the chapter's evaporation activities where only water disappears and salt remains.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing chemical change shows the student does not distinguish between physical change (change of state, reversible) and chemical change; the chapter explicitly frames evaporation as a physical change.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose option C can be redirected by asking what they observed in the china-dish heating activity — whether the residue looked like a new substance or like familiar salt. Students who prefer a step-by-step account can be asked to narrate what happens to the water molecules as the paper warms up, drawing on the chapter's definition of evaporation.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evaporation as the conversion of liquid water to water vapour and explain how this physical change of state separates a dissolved solid from a liquid, citing evidence from at least one observation.

competency.competency_text: Description of physical changes in matter

assessment_items.question_text: In coastal salt pans, seawater is collected in large shallow pits and left in sunlight for several days. Salt is eventually collected from the floor of the pits. Why must the pits be shallow rather than deep?

options.label: A
options.text: Shallow pits allow the salt to be filtered through the sandy floor more easily

options.label: B
options.text: Shallow pits expose a larger surface area of water to sunlight and air, allowing water to evaporate faster

options.label: C
options.text: Shallow pits keep the water at a lower temperature so the salt does not dissolve further

options.label: D
options.text: Shallow pits prevent the salt from sinking to the bottom before it can be collected

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing filtration through the floor conflates two chapter methods — evaporation and filtration — showing the student has not yet attached the salt-pan context specifically to the evaporation mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'prevent salt from sinking' shows a misconception that salt settles by gravity like sand; the chapter is explicit that salt is dissolved and does not sediment.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing lower temperature to prevent further dissolving shows an inverted causal reasoning — lower temperature would slow evaporation, not help it, and misattributes the purpose of the design to solubility control rather than evaporation rate.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose filtration through the floor may benefit from revisiting the china-dish activity and being asked whether a deeper dish would have made the process faster or slower. Students who are comfortable with the concept can be extended by asking what role wind plays in the salt pans, connecting it to the winnowing unit's use of moving air.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate evaporation as a physical change that separates dissolved solids
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe evaporation as the conversion of liquid water to water vapour and explain how this physical change of state separates a dissolved solid from a liquid, citing evidence from at least one observation.

competency.competency_text: Description of physical changes in matter

assessment_items.question_text: A student heats a salt solution in a china dish over a spirit lamp. She observes steam rising from the dish and the liquid level dropping. Eventually, only a white dry solid remains in the dish. Describe what physical change occurred to the water during this process and explain why this method successfully separates salt from water while filtration could not.
expected_elements: The water underwent a physical change of state — it converted from liquid water into water vapour (steam), which escaped into the air.
This change of state is called evaporation; it is a physical change because no new substance is formed and the water vapour could condense back to liquid water.
Filtration cannot separate salt from water because dissolved salt particles are too small to be retained by the filter paper's pores and pass straight through with the water.
Evaporation works for this separation because it removes the liquid component entirely by converting it to vapour, leaving only the solid salt behind.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to compare evaporation and filtration in a single response can first answer each question separately: 'What happens to the water?' and 'Why doesn't filtration work for salt?' before combining their answers. Students with stronger reasoning can be asked to add one sentence about whether the change is reversible or not, reinforcing the physical-change concept.

assessment_items.question_text: A student tests five objects with a bar magnet. Refer to the table provided. Based on these results, which two objects would be successfully removed from a mixture of all five using only a magnet?

options.label: A
options.text: Aluminium foil and copper coin

options.label: B
options.text: Iron nail and aluminium foil

options.label: C
options.text: Iron nail and steel pin

options.label: D
options.text: Steel pin and copper coin

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing iron nail and aluminium foil shows the student used 'metal' as a proxy for 'magnetic', failing to distinguish between magnetic metals (iron, steel) and non-magnetic metals (aluminium, copper).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing steel pin and copper coin shows a partial correct choice (steel pin) paired with an incorrect choice (copper coin), suggesting the student is guessing one answer rather than reading the table systematically.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing aluminium foil and copper coin shows the student may be selecting by some other property (both are shiny, flat, or associated with everyday objects) rather than reading the magnetic response column.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose aluminium foil can be asked to predict what would happen if they actually brought a magnet close to a piece of aluminium foil — this ground-truth check redirects to empirical observation. Students who benefit from verbal reasoning can be asked to read the table aloud and circle only the rows with 'Yes' before selecting their answer.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: Large cranes fitted with magnets are used at industrial scrap yards to separate iron from heaps of mixed waste. Which physical property of iron makes this industrial separation method effective?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron dissolves in rainwater and is later recovered by evaporating the collected water

options.label: B
options.text: Iron has a larger particle size than the other materials in the heap, so it cannot pass through the crane's mesh

options.label: C
options.text: Iron is a magnetic substance that is attracted to and held by a magnetic field

options.label: D
options.text: Iron is much heavier than the other waste materials, so it sinks to the bottom of the heap

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'heavier and sinks' shows the student is applying the density/sedimentation principle from the decantation section to a solid-solid mixture context where gravity-based settling is not the operative mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing particle size shows the student is mapping the sieving/filtration principle onto this scenario, confusing a magnetic force mechanism with a physical-barrier mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing dissolving and evaporation shows a conceptually disconnected response — the student is retrieving the evaporation method from the dissolved-salt context and misapplying it to a metallic solid that does not dissolve in water.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose density can be asked whether the magnet needs to touch the iron to pick it up, or whether it can attract the iron from a distance — this draws attention to the force-at-a-distance character of magnetism that distinguishes it from gravity-based methods. Students who prefer to reason from familiar examples can think of the nail-and-sawdust activity and be asked which property of the nail the magnet was responding to.

assessment_items.stage_label: Investigate magnetic separation and extend the property-to-method classification
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify substances as magnetic or non-magnetic based on observed response to a magnet and can populate a complete property-to-method map that correctly assigns all nine chapter separation methods to the physical property each exploits.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Method | Physical property exploited
Handpicking | ?
Winnowing | ?
Sieving | ?
Sedimentation and Decantation | ?
Filtration | ?
Evaporation | ?
Churning | ?
Magnetic separation | ?
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. For each separation method listed, write the physical property of the mixture components that makes the method effective. Use the following property terms: size difference, density or weight difference, particle size relative to pore size, solubility difference (physical change of state), magnetic character.
expected_elements: Handpicking — size difference (and visible colour or shape difference allowing manual distinction).
Winnowing — density or weight difference (lighter components carried by air, heavier fall).
Sieving — size difference between particles and mesh holes (particles larger than holes are retained).
Sedimentation and Decantation — density difference (heavier insoluble components settle to the bottom).
Filtration — particle size relative to pore size (particles larger than pores are retained on filter paper).
Evaporation — solubility difference and physical change of state (liquid converts to vapour, dissolved solid remains).
Churning — density difference (lighter component floats to surface and is skimmed off).
Magnetic separation — magnetic character (magnetic substances attracted to magnet; non-magnetic are not).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who confuse sieving and filtration (both are size-based) can be asked to compare the two methods in terms of the state of the mixture — sieving operates on solid-solid mixtures, filtration on solid-liquid — and note whether this changes the relevant property description. Students who find the table format challenging can first sort the methods into 'size-based', 'density-based', 'state-change-based', and 'magnetic-based' groups verbally before writing property terms.

assessment_items.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can select and apply the appropriate separation method for a given mixture by identifying the decisive observable physical property difference between its components — including size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — and can justify why an alternative method would be less effective for that mixture.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: A cook wants to separate bran from wheat flour after grinding. The bran pieces are larger than the fine flour particles. Which method is most appropriate, and why would filtration through a wet filter paper be a poor alternative?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporation is most appropriate because the moisture in the flour must be removed first; filtration would leave bran in the flour

options.label: B
options.text: Magnetic separation is most appropriate because bran contains iron from the wheat plant; filtration would separate by the wrong property

options.label: C
options.text: Sieving is most appropriate because it separates by size difference between particles and mesh holes; wet filtration would make the flour paste up and clog the paper, but more importantly, filtration is designed for solid-liquid mixtures, not dry solid-solid mixtures

options.label: D
options.text: Winnowing is most appropriate because bran is lighter than flour; filtration would work equally well but is slower

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing winnowing shows the student is applying a weight/density method to a scenario where size difference is the decisive property; the student may have recalled that husk and grain are separated by air and generalised without checking the property.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing magnetic separation for bran shows the student is pattern-matching to a solid-solid mixture (as in the iron-and-sawdust example) without checking whether either component has magnetic character.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing evaporation shows the student is applying a dissolved-solid method to a solid-solid mixture, revealing a fundamental mismatch between the mixture type and the method's operating conditions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose winnowing can be asked whether flour and bran differ primarily in weight or in size when they have felt both between their fingers — grounding the property identification in a tactile observation. Students who are confident with the correct answer can be extended by asking what additional method would be needed if a small quantity of iron filings were also present in the mixture.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can select and apply the appropriate separation method for a given mixture by identifying the decisive observable physical property difference between its components — including size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — and can justify why an alternative method would be less effective for that mixture.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: A student has a mixture containing iron filings, common salt, and sand. She wants to recover all three components separately. Which sequence of methods is correct, and what is the decisive reason the magnetic step must come before the evaporation step?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaporate first, then filter, then use magnet — because evaporation removes water, making the remaining solid easier to handle

options.label: B
options.text: Filter first, then use magnet, then evaporate — because filtration separates all three solids from each other before any further steps are needed

options.label: C
options.text: Use magnet first, then add water and filter, then evaporate — because if salt is evaporated first, the iron filings become embedded in the salt residue and cannot be magnetically removed cleanly

options.label: D
options.text: Use magnet first, then evaporate, then filter — because evaporation separates sand from salt before filtration is applied

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing evaporation first shows the student has not reasoned through what happens to the iron filings when water is removed — the filings would be mixed into the salt crust, blocking the subsequent magnetic step.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing filtration first shows the student believes filtration can separate three solids from each other; this reflects a misunderstanding of filtration as a solid-liquid method, not a solid-solid separation tool.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing magnet first then evaporate then filter is partially correct on the first step but wrong on the subsequent order — evaporation after removing iron would convert the salt-sand-water mixture and leave sand and salt residue together, with no remaining liquid for filtration to act on.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who chose option A can be asked to visualise the china dish after evaporation: would the iron filings be floating free or buried in the salt layer? This concrete visualisation redirects them to sequence reasoning. Students who are comfortable with the reasoning can be extended by asking what would happen if the student used decantation instead of filtration in step two, and whether it would fully remove the sand.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can select and apply the appropriate separation method for a given mixture by identifying the decisive observable physical property difference between its components — including size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — and can justify why an alternative method would be less effective for that mixture.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.question_text: A classmate claims: 'Decantation is just a slower version of filtration — they both separate solids from liquids, so you could always use one instead of the other.' Do you agree or disagree with this claim? Justify your answer by explaining the physical property each method relies on and describing a mixture for which decantation works but filtration is unnecessary, and a mixture for which filtration is needed but decantation alone is insufficient.
look_for: The response disagrees with the claim and distinguishes the two methods by their operative property: decantation relies on density difference causing the solid to settle by gravity, while filtration relies on particle size relative to pore size to physically block particles.

The response identifies that decantation can work for large, heavy insoluble particles (e.g., coarse sand or oil in water) where particles settle completely and the upper liquid is sufficiently clear.

The response identifies that filtration is needed when particles are too fine to settle fully by decantation, citing that the filtrate after decantation can still appear cloudy with very fine suspended particles.
The response correctly treats these as two distinct mechanisms, not as fast and slow versions of the same process, and does not conflate them as interchangeable.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find open-ended disagreement prompts difficult can be told: 'Think about what property decantation uses and what property filtration uses — are they the same?' This frames the task as a property comparison rather than an abstract argument. Students who are confident in the distinction can be extended by asking whether the two methods could ever be used in sequence on the same mixture (as in the sedimentation-then-filtration activity), and what advantage that sequence offers over using filtration alone from the start.

assessment_items.stage_label: Select and justify the appropriate separation method for a given mixture
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can select and apply the appropriate separation method for a given mixture by identifying the decisive observable physical property difference between its components — including size, density, solubility, and magnetic character — and can justify why an alternative method would be less effective for that mixture.

competency.competency_text: Classification of matter by observable physical characteristics

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Mixture | Components | Property difference(s) present | Best method | Decisive property | Alternative method tried | Why alternative is less effective
A: Ocean water at the coast | Water + dissolved salt | ? | ? | ? | ? | ?
B: Workshop floor sweepings | Iron filings + sawdust | ? | ? | ? | ? | ?
C: Kitchen waste water | Sand + oil + water | ? | ? | ? | ? | ?
D: Post-harvest grain pile | Grain + husk + small stones | ? | ? | ? | ? | ?
assessment_items.task: Four separation challenges are described in the table provided. For each mixture, complete all columns: identify the property difference(s) present between the components, select the best separation method, name the decisive property that method exploits, name one alternative method someone might try, and explain — using a specific property mismatch — why that alternative is less effective for this mixture.
assessment_items.scaffold: Before filling in each row, ask yourself: What are the components? How do they differ in size, density, solubility, or magnetic character? Which of those differences is the most useful handle for a separation method? Then consider: if someone grabbed the wrong method from the list, which property difference would that method fail to exploit in this mixture?
format_of_output: Completed table with all seven columns filled for all four mixture rows
One sentence of justification for the 'Why alternative is less effective' column in each row — the justification must name a specific property mismatch, not just say the alternative 'would not work'

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires simultaneous reasoning across both central operations — classifying by observable physical property and selecting the method that exploits that property — and a classification table with justification is the most direct vehicle for demonstrating both in a single, observable response.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can identify the decisive physical property difference in a given mixture, map that property to the appropriate separation method, and evaluate an alternative method by identifying the specific property mismatch that makes it less effective — integrating classification reasoning (C-1.1) with physical-change reasoning (C-1.2 for mixture C's oil-water layer and mixture A's evaporation) in a single analytical act.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold is a thinking prompt, not a template — it directs the student's reasoning process before writing, not the format of their output. The table structure is the output format. A teacher reading the responses should look at whether the 'decisive property' column names a specific physical property (not just the method), and whether the 'why alternative is less effective' justification argues from a property mismatch rather than from practicality alone.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: Name a specific property difference for every row (e.g., 'magnetic character' not just 'because iron sticks to magnets'); select the best method correctly in all four rows; write a 'why alternative fails' sentence that explicitly names the property the alternative method cannot exploit for that mixture (e.g., 'Filtration would not remove dissolved salt because salt particles are smaller than any filter pore'). Weak responses: Leave property columns vague ('they are different'); select plausible but incorrect methods in one or more rows; justify the alternative failure with 'it would be too slow' or 'it would not work' without naming a property mismatch.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the table format overwhelming can be guided to complete just two rows first — choosing the most familiar mixtures (ocean water and workshop sweepings) — and then attempt the remaining rows. Students who are confident with all four rows can be asked to add a fifth row of their own invention, creating a mixture where two methods are equally valid and explaining under what condition one would be preferred over the other.
